To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the integration of basic sciences into medical education is beneficial for knowledge retention and transfer.
The inclusion of basic science in a medical school curriculum may improve diagnostic accuracy, but the mechanism behind this is not clear.

(a) teaching basic science improves diagnostic accuracy; (b) this effect is due to the ability to identify distinguishing features of the disease; (c) the effect of basic science is greatest in diseases with clear causal linkages with basic sciences; (d) basic science may not be the only tool to improve the identification of distinguishing features.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the integration of basic and clinical sciences, and how this may impact the development of clinical skills.
the role of science in the medical curriculum, and the benefits that can be gained by integrating science with medicine.
the integration of basic and clinical sciences, and how they are taught.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
basic science should only be integrated where it facilitates clinical reasoning, or where it helps to construct causal pathways.
basic science should only be integrated where it is useful for the learner, where it facilitates retention or transfer.
basic science should continue to be taught, but that it should be taught in ways that help learners construct clinical causal pathways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

basic science is valuable in the context of medical education, but that the specific content of the basic science taught should be tailored to the context of clinical problems, and the learning objectives.
basic science is a tool to improve clinical decision making.
basic science should not be taught for its own sake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
basic science is not a one size fits all solution to medical education problems.
basic science can be used to help students develop diagnostic reasoning, and this is most effective in conditions where there are strong causal links between basic science and clinical presentations.
basic science can be taught effectively in the context of clinical cases, but that the content should be chosen to help learners construct causal pathways.
